blacklist.note: Lexical entries are cheap to check and catch roughly the easy 80%. The structural entries are what actually survived four rounds of model review on 2026-08-14, because each message passed inspection on its own. Both lists are time-dated detectors and will drift; re-profile them against real sent mail rather than treating them as permanent.

structural.why: Appeared in five of the eight messages sent on 2026-08-13/14. The single strongest tell in our own corpus. Name one capability, the one this recipient would care about.

structural.pattern: First name followed by an em-dash as the opener
structural.why: All eight sent messages opened this way. Vary the entry into the first sentence, not just its content.

structural.pattern: Question that supplies its own answer options
structural.example: spreadsheets, another system, or something homegrown?
structural.why: Started as a good idea for lowering reply effort, then became the default closer. A menu tells the recipient you already decided what the answers are.
Two of three drafts in one batch ended on this exact rhythm. Fine once; a tic across a batch.

structural.pattern: Not just X, but Y / Not only X, but also Y / Not X. Y.
structural.why: Negative parallelism. Among the most reliable machine-writing signals.

structural.pattern: Whether you're X or Y / While X, Y is also important
structural.why: Hedged symmetry. Addresses every reader at once, which means it addresses none of them.

structural.pattern: Copula inflation: serves as, stands as, represents, marks
structural.why: Keep the verb when it enumerates, defines, or locates. Replace it when it only inflates a plain 'is'.

structural.pattern: This is where X comes in / At its core / When it comes to
structural.why: Generic connective scaffolding with no information in it.

structural.pattern: Restating the company's About page back at them
structural.why: Reads as research theatre. They know what they do. Use the research to ask a question only someone who read it could ask.

structural.pattern: Rule-of-three parallelism anywhere in the message
structural.why: In a message under 60 words, a tricolon is almost always cadence standing in for a point.

blacklist.batchRule: Outside the exact required footer and required on-site origin idea, no content phrase of three or more words may repeat across a batch, and no two messages may share a first-sentence structure. Check message-specific copy across the batch, never per message: every convergent batch we have produced passed per-message review.

examples.situation: The company makes several soil blends and the recipient owns operations. The sender is unsure how production is currently planned.
examples.subject: production planning
examples.body: Hey Sam — came across Ridge Soil while looking at smaller soil manufacturers. Looks like you make quite a few different blends. Not sure how you plan production when ingredient availability changes, but I'm curious what you use today. I'm building operations software for smaller manufacturers and trying to understand where the spreadsheets start to break.

examples.situation: The product catalog shows the same blends sold in several package sizes. Ask a narrow operational question without asserting that a problem exists.
examples.subject: bag sizes
examples.body: Hey Mia — saw that Mesa Growers sells the same mixes in a bunch of bag sizes. Do the recipes and packaging materials live in the same system for you, or is that still split across a few places? I'm working on this exact problem for smaller batch manufacturers, so I figured it was worth asking.

examples.situation: The company publishes many ingredient-heavy products, but there is no evidence about its software. Lead with honest uncertainty.
examples.subject: raw materials
examples.body: Hey Chris — I found North Fork while researching smaller fertilizer and soil producers. You have enough different products that I wondered how you keep raw-material availability tied to what can actually be made. You may already have this handled cleanly. If not, I'd be curious what holds it together today.

examples.situation: Research confirms the company uses Xero, but does not confirm how it manages production. Ask about the boundary between accounting and operations.
examples.subject: outside xero
examples.body: Hey Jordan — looks like Cedar Works uses Xero. I'm curious what you use for the operational side before bills and invoices get there — inventory, purchasing, and production. I'm building software for manufacturers that want to keep Xero as the accounting system, and I'm trying to understand how much still lives in spreadsheets.

examples.situation: The company buys bulky ingredients from multiple suppliers. The message explores freight allocation without claiming its costs are inaccurate.
examples.subject: inbound freight
examples.body: Hey Taylor — quick question after looking through Valley Blend's product line: when a truck brings in several ingredients, how do you split the freight into the actual cost of each one? We ran into that problem with a soil manufacturer and it got messy fast. I'm curious whether you have a clean way to handle it.

examples.situation: The company describes batch production and lot-tracked products publicly. Ask how the operator connects consumed ingredients to finished output.
examples.subject: batch records
examples.body: Hey Alex — saw that Prairie Organics produces in batches and tracks finished lots. How are you connecting the ingredient lots used in a run to the finished product today? I'm building an ERP around these smaller manufacturing workflows and would genuinely like to know what works for you.

examples.situation: The company ships palletized products and publishes freight information. Ask about the handoff from sales order to warehouse paperwork.
examples.subject: shipping paperwork
examples.body: Hey Morgan — looks like a lot of your orders leave by pallet or truck. I'm curious what happens between the sales order and the loading instructions or BOL. Is that one workflow for you, or does the warehouse end up rebuilding the details somewhere else?

examples.situation: A strongly qualified owner may be using spreadsheets, but that is not publicly verified. Offer a useful review instead of asking directly for a meeting.
examples.subject: your spreadsheets
examples.body: Hey Jamie — I'm building an ERP for smaller batch manufacturers, initially soil and fertilizer companies. If purchasing, inventory, or production still runs through spreadsheets at Green County, I'd be happy to map one of those workflows into Ashicore and tell you honestly whether it fits. Useful, or are you already set?

examples.situation: Only segment fit and the recipient role are verified. Keep the email modest rather than manufacturing fake personalization.
examples.subject: operations question
examples.body: Hey Casey — I'm talking with people who run smaller batch manufacturing businesses. Ashicore came out of dealing with the inventory and production work that tends to sit between spreadsheets and accounting software. Not sure if that describes your setup at all, but what do you use to run it today?

examples.situation: One follow-up to an unanswered operational question. Add no new claim or pressure.
examples.subject: Re: production planning
examples.body: Hey Sam — just following up in case this got buried. Still curious how you handle production planning today.

replyExamples.situation: A soil formulator at a small, established soil-amendment manufacturer replied to an initial outreach message by asking whether Ashicore is an app for formulas. Public research showed bagged and bulk blends, custom formulas, wholesale distribution, and a small team. The response has not yet produced an observable outcome.
replyExamples.inbound: Are you building a app for the formulas?
replyExamples.body:
Yeah — formulas are a big part of it. You add the ingredients for each blend, and Ashicore figures out what you need for a batch, tracks what you actually use, and keeps your inventory and costs up to date. It also keeps the old versions whenever a formula changes.

We're working closely with our first few manufacturers, so if it looks like a good fit for LGM, we'll set up your products and formulas for you at no cost and let you try it with your own data.

What are you using to manage all of that right now?

Azure Eller | Ashicore
ashicore.app
Ashicore LLC · PO Box 593 · Paonia, CO 81428
Business outreach — to opt out, reply "no" and I won't contact you again.

learningCases.context: The recipient was LGM's soil formulator. Research supported a highly specific formula-and-orders message.
learningCases.approach: The initial email led with detailed observations and several operational questions, then referred to Ashicore only as something being built for shops like theirs.
learningCases.observedOutcome: The recipient replied, 'Are you building a app for the formulas?'
learningCases.interpretation: The specificity earned attention, but the recipient still had to infer what Ashicore was. This is evidence for testing clearer product framing, not proof that every first email needs the same framing or founder story.
learningCases.untestedAlternative:
Sam — my family runs an organic potting-soil company, and I built Ashicore to keep formulas, production, and inventory in one place.

Since you handle LGM's formulas, what are you using today—spreadsheets, another system, or something homegrown?
learningCases.caution: This alternative is preserved as a record of what was proposed, not as a model to copy. It contains three of the structural patterns now on the blacklist: the em-dash opener, the three-noun list, and the answer-menu question.

learningCases.context: Three drafts were run through a four-pass loop: Codex drafted, Claude critiqued the batch, Codex revised, a fresh Claude challenged the result. A batch-level diversity rule had already been added after an earlier round converged.
learningCases.approach: Add more review and more explicit diversity rules each time the output looked templated.
learningCases.observedOutcome: Every round produced messages whose first sentences shared a structure, and five of eight sent messages carried the same three-noun capability list. The owner's read: 'they still seem a bit AI to me.' The run log records Codex noting that Claude had proposed more varied openings which Codex then 'improved' back into one shape.
learningCases.interpretation: The review loop caused this. Preference-trained models carry a typicality bias: given two options of equal quality they favor the more familiar one, so each judging pass moves a batch toward the median. Adding review rounds to fix blandness makes it worse. This is a known mechanism, not a quirk of these particular prompts.
learningCases.changeApplied: Replaced the review loop with distribution-level candidate generation (five candidates with probabilities in one call, selecting off the mode) plus a mechanical pre-send check that fires or does not fire rather than offering an opinion.
learningCases.openQuestion: Whether lower-probability candidates actually reply better. Borrowed from research on other generation tasks; unmeasured for cold email. The run log records the chosen candidate's probability so this can eventually be answered.
